Chapter Five: Neglect at Home—The Cost of Ignoring Citizens’ Needs
Picture this: a crowded emergency room buzzing with urgency. A nurse moves quickly, bouncing from patient to patient, trying to do her best with what little she’s got. She recognizes so many faces—folks who just can’t afford regular care, parents juggling multiple jobs but still unable to make ends meet, kids struggling with chronic health problems. And every shift, that frustration grows a little deeper. It’s hard not to notice: while billions are poured into military operations far from home, basic needs here in her own community are left unmet.
Most of us don’t really see the connection between what happens overseas and what’s missing in our neighborhoods. The nurse thinks about her neighbor who lost his job when the local factory shut down—a decision made by someone miles away, based on shifting economic priorities. He tried to get help, but the process was slow, confusing, and honestly, kind of discouraging. Soon, his family fell behind on rent, and the stress started to affect their health in ways no doctor could easily fix.
The nurse can’t help but wonder—why do we spend so much energy on conflicts thousands of miles away, while families right here are left to struggle alone?
You don’t have to look far to see the signs of neglect. Roads and bridges falling apart. Schools scraping by on shoestring budgets. More people living without stable homes. She talks with teachers who have to buy classroom supplies with their own money, and social workers who can barely keep up with overwhelming caseloads.
The government likes to talk about freedom and opportunity, but for many, that promise feels out of reach. The gap between rich and poor keeps growing, and the hope for a better life drifts further away.
Meanwhile, big decisions are made behind closed doors—by people who might never have struggled to pay a medical bill or worried about their next paycheck. Policies get shaped by lobbyists and special interests, while the voices of the most vulnerable are pushed aside.
The nurse sees it firsthand—patients putting off care because they just can’t afford it, families forced to choose between buying medicine or putting food on the table.
What many folks don’t realize is how tightly linked our domestic and foreign policies really are. Every dollar spent on war or military contracts is a dollar not spent on healthcare, education, or vital social services. Politicians talk about sacrifice and patriotism, but let’s be honest—the hardest sacrifices always seem to fall on those who already have the least.
The real cost of neglect isn’t just about money—it’s personal. The nurse sees the toll it takes on people’s mental health, on families trying to stay together, and on a community’s sense of trust. People start to lose faith in their leaders, and in the promise that hard work will actually pay off. And the nurse finds herself asking: how long can a country keep ignoring its own people before the cracks become too deep to fix?
As her shift finally ends, the nurse pauses to reflect. What would it look like to truly serve our own? It’s not just about budgets or policies—it’s about what we value most. A strong society invests in its future by caring for those who are most at risk, making sure everyone gets a fair shot. When that commitment fades, even the mightiest nation can find itself on shaky ground.
